concepts.name: SQLite WAL checkpointing
concepts.reason: The packet defines checkpointing as transferring WAL transactions into the database and describes its progress, completion, and reset behavior.

concepts.name: Automatic checkpoint triggers
concepts.reason: The packet specifies the default threshold, connection-close behavior, configuration options, and PASSIVE mode for automatic checkpoints.

concepts.name: Checkpoint modes
concepts.reason: The packet describes PASSIVE, FULL, RESTART, TRUNCATE, and NOOP behavior and their blocking conditions.

concepts.name: Checkpoint locking and progress
concepts.reason: The packet explains checkpoint locks, reader and writer interactions, partial progress, and starvation conditions.

claims.text: A checkpoint transfers transactions from the WAL file back into the original database.
claims.quote: Moving the WAL file transactions back into the database is called a " checkpoint ".

claims.text: The default automatic checkpoint threshold is 1000 pages.
claims.quote: By default, SQLite does a checkpoint automatically when the WAL file reaches a threshold size of 1000 pages.

claims.text: A checkpoint may run concurrently with readers but must stop before overwriting a page beyond a current reader's end mark.
claims.quote: A checkpoint can run concurrently with readers, however the checkpoint must stop when it reaches a page in the WAL that is past the end mark of any current reader.

claims.text: Before moving WAL content into the database, the WAL must be synced to persistent storage.
claims.quote: The WAL must be synced to persistent storage prior to moving content from the WAL into the database

claims.text: Frequent checkpoints favor read performance, while infrequent checkpoints amortize checkpoint cost across more writes.
claims.quote: To maximize the read performance, one wants to keep the WAL as small as possible and hence run checkpoints frequently, perhaps as often as every COMMIT.

claims.text: Automatic checkpointing also occurs when the last database connection closes.
claims.quote: By default, SQLite will automatically checkpoint whenever a COMMIT occurs that causes the WAL file to be 1000 pages or more in size, or when the last database connection on a database file closes.

claims.text: Automatic checkpointing can be disabled with a zero or negative N value to sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint().
claims.quote: Passing zero or a negative value as the N parameter disables automatic checkpoints entirely.

claims.text: Automatic checkpoints initiated by sqlite3_wal_autocheckpoint() use PASSIVE mode.
claims.quote: Checkpoints initiated by this mechanism are PASSIVE . Every new database connection defaults to having the auto-checkpoint enabled with a threshold of 1000 or SQLITE_DEFAULT_WAL_AUTOCHECKPOINT pages.

claims.text: PASSIVE checkpoints do as much work as possible without waiting for readers or writers and can remain unfinished when either is concurrent.
claims.quote: Checkpoint as many frames as possible without waiting for any database readers or writers to finish, then sync the database file if all frames in the log were checkpointed.

claims.text: FULL checkpoints wait until there is no writer and all readers use the most recent database snapshot, then checkpoint and sync the log.
claims.quote: This mode blocks (it invokes the busy-handler callback ) until there is no database writer and all readers are reading from the most recent database snapshot.

claims.text: RESTART adds a wait for all readers to use only the database file, ensuring the next writer restarts the WAL from its beginning.
claims.quote: This ensures that the next writer will restart the log file from the beginning.

claims.text: TRUNCATE behaves like RESTART and truncates the log to zero bytes before successful return.
claims.quote: This mode works the same way as SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART with the addition that it also truncates the log file to zero bytes just prior to a successful return.

claims.text: NOOP checkpoints zero frames and can be used to read log and checkpointed frame counts through output parameters.
claims.quote: The only reason to invoke a NOOP checkpoint is to access the values returned by sqlite3_wal_checkpoint_v2() via output parameters *pnLog and *pnCkpt.

claims.text: Every checkpoint call obtains an exclusive checkpoint lock; if another process holds a checkpoint operation, the call returns SQLITE_BUSY without invoking the busy handler.
claims.quote: All calls obtain an exclusive "checkpoint" lock on the database file. If any other process is running a checkpoint operation at the same time, the lock cannot be obtained and SQLITE_BUSY is returned.

claims.text: FULL, RESTART, and TRUNCATE also obtain an exclusive writer lock.
claims.quote: The SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_FULL, RESTART and TRUNCATE modes also obtain the exclusive "writer" lock on the database file.

claims.text: If the busy handler gives up before a writer lock or reader wait completes, the operation continues like PASSIVE and returns SQLITE_BUSY.
claims.quote: If the busy-handler returns 0 before the writer lock is obtained or while waiting for database readers, the checkpoint operation proceeds from that point in the same way as SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE - checkpointing as many frames as possible without blocking any further.

claims.text: Overlapping readers can prevent every checkpoint from completing, causing unbounded WAL growth.
claims.quote: However, if a database has many concurrent overlapping readers and there is always at least one active reader, then no checkpoints will be able to complete and hence the WAL file will grow without bound.

claims.text: Reader gaps, when no processes read the database, allow checkpoints an opportunity to complete.
claims.quote: This scenario can be avoided by ensuring that there are "reader gaps": times when no processes are reading from the database and that checkpoints are attempted during those times.

claims.text: The database file must be synced before the WAL is reset.
claims.quote: the database file must be synced prior to resetting the WAL.

claims.text: Since SQLite 3.11.0, a single transaction's WAL size should be proportional to the transaction, with each changed page written once.
claims.quote: As of SQLite version 3.11.0 (2016-02-15), the WAL file for a single transaction should be proportional in size to the transaction itself. Pages that are changed by the transaction should only be written into the WAL file once.

handoffs.name: WAL reader concurrency
handoffs.reason: Reader end marks and overlapping read transactions affect checkpoint progress; the topic is outside the checkpointing concept boundary.

limitations: Only the supplied source packet was used; it does not establish expert disagreements or a broad history of changing interpretations.
Three deepening passes were completed, but each added claims at a rate above 5%; the hard pass budget prevents a saturation conclusion.
The packet mentions older SQLite behavior before version 3.11.0 but does not explain its causes beyond repeated writes of a page when a transaction exceeds the page cache.
